[sec.4, p.7] The subjunctive is always stressed on the penultimate syllable, and should not be confused with the jussive, which is stressed on the final syllable and is used mainly for wishes and commands ... [sec.5.2, p.9] There are two genders: masculine (m.) and feminine (f.). tone_statements.citation: Tajebe, Esayas (2015). Descriptive Grammar of Saaho. Addis Ababa University. xiv+370 pp.
tone_statements.quote: we have described the facts in Saaho to show that it is tonal-accent language. When we look the placement of tone accent at word level, high tone is restricted to either the ultimate or penultimate mora, not to a syllable position. Here if the high tone is on the penultimate following mora bear low tone. ... When we consider surface realization of short vowels at word level, we can distinguish two level tones, High and none high. But with long vowels there are three underlying tonal patterns High, High-Low, and Low-High which can be realized as falling and rising tones. ... The tone has both lexical and grammatical functions in Saaho.
tone_statements.summary: Tone-accent: H vs non-high, H on final or penultimate mora; long-vowel HL/LH surface falling/rising; lexical and grammatical (gender, mood, case); floating L (question, accusative); downstep noted.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the deciding B&V 2005 passages are verbatim at the stated PDF pages in the copy consulted. The classification (contrastive, morphologically placed pitch accent on penult/final; tonal-OR-pitch accent, not weight-sensitive, right edge, word domain) is independently stated by the held 370-pp reference grammar (Esayas 2015 sec. 2.2.3: tone-accent, H restricted to final or penultimate mora, lexical + grammatical, unaccented words) and by three sources downloaded now: Welmers 1952:147 primary text (lexical + morphological 'stress' realized as highest pitch, many stems unaccented), B&V 2010 EAE p.469 (summarizing Hayward 1997: pitch accent, one tone-bearing syllable per word, NP sandhi) and B&V 2017 p.68 (m. H-L vs f. L-H). Nothing ties accent to syllable weight in any of them. The only unheld tone-specific works (Hayward 1983, 1997) are print-only and, per the authors who cite them

sources.citation: Welmers, William E. (1952). Notes on the structure of Saho. Word 8: 145-162, 236-251.
sources.quote: 'Stress in different positions is obviously the determining factor in contrasts such as those between |yibáda| my son and |yibadá| my daughter ... the stressed vowel has the highest pitch, and the form ends with low pitch. But forms that are not clearly stressed on a vowel before the last one are pronounced in isolation with a final high pitch ... may also be interpreted as conditioned by an absence of stress in the form ... forms with fewer than two stresses are interpreted as having either stress with a vowel other than the last, or no stress ... stress has both a lexical and a morphological

sources.citation: Banti, Giorgio & Moreno Vergari (2017). Aspects of Saho dialectology. Quaderni di Vicino Oriente XII (Afroasiatica Romana): 65-93.
sources.quote: 'Pitch is used morphologically, e.g., in the opposition between m. H-L vs. f. L-H on the two final syllables of many nouns: Sa. Af. báɖa son vs. baɖá daughter ... Most m. nouns ending in short -a have a H-toned nom. and gen. in -í.'
sources.venue: Quaderni di Vicino Oriente XII (Afroasiatica Romana): 65-93

sources.citation: Banti, Giorgio & Moreno Vergari (2010). Saho language. In S. Uhlig (ed.), Encyclopaedia Aethiopica vol. 4, 468-471. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.
sources.quote: 'Hayward (1997: 69ff.) describes central and southern S. varieties as having a system of pitch accent with either high or low tones on short vowels and also falling and rising tones on long vowels. Only one syllable generally bears a high, falling or rising tone in each word, and tonal sandhi operates within complex noun phrases (NPs).'

sources.note: The catalog record for Saho (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements; Salt 1814 adds nothing on stress. Salt's 'Shiho' is the Saho of the Massawa/Arkiko hinterland (he names the Torua tribes Edo, Gumeddo, Begiddo, Assala-iddo and says the Hazorta speak the same language, p. 440), i.e. this is the right language but the work is a 1810 traveller's wordlist only. Opened via archive.org copies of the same 1814 edition because HathiTrust blocked the download.
